newsitem.title: PERU: Health of Peru hostages grows more fragile daily.
newsitem.headline: Health of Peru hostages grows more fragile daily.

text.p: After six weeks in captivity, VIP hostages held by Peruvian rebels show deepening signs of physical and mental strain, which is intensifying pressure on the government and guerrillas to end the crisis quickly.
Aid workers and police said in interviews that most hostages in the Japanese ambassador's home are being treated for ailments such as hypertension, digestive problems or depression.
"There are varying conditions of health but almost all are now on medication," Red Cross spokesman Ruben Ortega told Reuters.
Both sides, while unyielding over the rebel demand to free 400 jailed comrades, have sought to avoid harming the hostages.

A death among the hostages would be a political blow to President Alberto Fujimori, who has been praised at home and abroad for his resolve in not caving in to rebel demands, and patience for not storming the residence.
However, a hurt hostage would also likely lessen any sympathy for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), which has vowed not to kill any of the hostages.
The hostages face the psychological strain of knowing that their captors, who mined and booby-trapped the compound and are training automatic weapons on them, have a history rife with violence.

And while the rebels were trained to undergo physical hardship in the central jungle areas of Peru, most of the captives are more accustomed to lavish cocktail parties of the kind the rebels stormed on Dec. 17.

"The guerrillas can stand it ... But can the hostages?" MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco has warned. "If they suffer, the Peruvian government must accept all responsibility for not facilitating a solution to this situation."
A Red Cross medical team enters daily to check on the health of the hostages, but will not elaborate on the health of the captives to avoid alarming family members.
"There is no immediate emergency situation," an official with the Japanese government task force said in an interview. "But every day is critical."
The last two hostages freed left for medical reasons. Early on Sunday, Gen. Jose Rivas Rodriguez, a deputy chief in Peru's national police, was carried out on a stretcher.
"He is improving but he still complains about the gastritis caused by so much tension," his son Javier said in an interview this week, adding that his father was also depressed.
The Lima College of Lawyers during the weekend published a message from former Supreme Court president and still captive Moises Pantoja written to his family from inside the residence.
"I can hardly walk. When I do, I lose my balance. My feet, hands and fingers have all gone hard. My arthritis stops me from reading and I can barely write," the message said.

A police source said in an interview that most of the 14 police officers held, generally higher ranking officers about 50 years old, were taking medication for such problems as hypertension and stomach ailments.
"The situation is complicated when you have 72 people in a small space every day for so many days," Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux said.

Jorge San Roman, Peru's 55-year-old deputy energy and mines minister, has shed 18 pounds (eight kg) from his previous 220 (100 kg) and jokes with his wife that this pleases him. "He says he is fine but has body pains because he sleeps on the floor," said his wife Martha, who receives two letters a week from him. "And he says he is fed up."
Provocative police tactics, including early morning march music blasted at the site and processions of armoured vehicles, have brought pressure on behalf of the captives from Japan.
"I'm worrying how it may affect the hostages inside. I'm wondering if I can ask ... the Peruvian government not to go too far," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said.
The rebels, who take the name for their movement from an 18th-century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, orginally seized hundreds of guests.

They released most but have kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, Fujimori's younger brother and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
